chunks: From him, from al-Abbas ibn 'Amir, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A gift (hiba) and an endowment (nihla) are [valid] as long as the owner has not died before taking possession. He said: 'It is inheritance.' If it is for a child under his guardianship, and he witnesses upon it, then it is valid.

key_terms.النِّحْلَةُ: Endowment or grant, often distinct from simple gift in legal nuance
key_terms.الْهِبَةُ: Gift, a voluntary transfer of property

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between hiba and nihla in Shia inheritance law when the donor dies before possession?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the validity of a gift (hiba) hinges on actual possession (qabda); if the donor dies before this transfer, the asset reverts to the general inheritance pool. The hadith further specifies a practical exception for minors, where a witnessed gift under guardianship remains valid, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on the completion of the contract through delivery. This distinction is crucial in determining whether an asset is distributed as a specific bequest or as part of the residual estate among heirs.
